claims.statement: His collation (盧校) deletes, supplies and emends graphs in the New Year audience passage, mostly agreeing with the Tongdian (e.g. 腢, 西入東出, 挾, 位, 南, 散, 獸, 倡, 獻), and judges 激沼水於殿下 superfluous.

translationRepairs: First, seal every yang portal, dress in black, and raise earthen dragons; second, station clay effigies and two ranks of boy dancers, altering the setup every seven days as statute prescribes.
Seal every yang portal, dress in black, and raise earthen dragons; [note 2] station clay effigies and two ranks of boy dancers, altering the setup every seven days as statute prescribes.
[一] and [二] are commentary-note markers, not an enumeration 'first ... second'.
Third, reverse the bindings, loop red cords around the soil altar, and beat the crimson drum.
Reverse the bindings, loop red cords around the soil altar, and beat the crimson drum.
Fourth, offer prayer and votive thanks with a pig-and-goat set, following canonical form.
Offer prayer and votive thanks with a pig-and-goat set, following canonical form.
For eight days shamans sun themselves in the open while snakes are assembled—per Dong Zhongshu's liturgy.
For eight days shamans sun themselves in the open while snakes are assembled.
The source sentence 暴巫聚蛇八日 has no mention of Dong Zhongshu; the attribution is an addition (the whole passage is already his).
Comment 2 quotes the Classic of Mountains and Seas: "northeast of the Great Wasteland rises Mount Xiongguangtuqiu.
Comment 2 quotes the Classic of Mountains and Seas: "northeast of the Great Wasteland rises a mountain called Xiongguang Tuqiu.
名曰凶廣土丘: the name is Xiongguang Tuqiu ('earthen hill'); received Shanhaijing texts read 凶犁土丘.
Huan Tan asks why clay dragons are fashioned when praying for rain.
I, Tan, asked: 'Why are clay dragons made when seeking rain?'
譚問 is Huan Tan's first-person narration within the New Discourses quotation.
Youxin's bride founded Yin; Jiang Yuan mothered Zhou—both golden ages rested on inner virtue.
the woman of Youxin made Yin flourish; Tai Jiang and Tai Ren mothered Zhou—both golden ages rested on inner virtue.
姜任 are Tai Jiang and Tai Ren, the Zhou matriarchs, not Jiang Yuan; 興殷 is 'made Yin flourish'.
The memorial opens with Directors Xiao and Ding and Masters Xu, Cheng, Pang, Mo, and Yi prostrate: "Your Majesty walks Qian and mirrors Kun; every motion harmonizes yin and yang.

The memorial opens with Director Xiao, Vice Director Ding, and Masters of Writing Xu, Cheng, Pang, Mo, and Yi prostrate: "Your Majesty walks Qian and mirrors Kun; every motion harmonizes yin and yang.
尚書令臣囂、僕射臣鼎: only Xiao is Director (令); Ding is Vice Director (僕射).
Comment 2 preserves Xia Qin's patent: "Yuanchu 6, third month, jiazi—the Grand Herald becomes Minister of Education.
Comment 2 preserves Xia Qin's patent: "Yuanchu 6, third month, jiazi—by edict Grand Herald Qin is made Minister over the Masses.
The patent names the appointee (大鴻臚勤) and is issued by edict (制詔); 司徒 is Minister over the Masses.
The Coachman Lan receives the case before the throne; female attendants pass it from Handmaid to Bright Companion to belt the empress.

The Palace Regular Attendant and Coachman of the Changle Palace, Lan, Marquis of Gaoxiang, kneels to receive the case before the throne; female attendants pass it from Handmaid to Bright Companion to belt the empress.
中常侍長樂(秋)太僕高鄉侯覽: offices and fief of the eunuch Lan (Hou Lan) are omitted; he kneels (長跪).
Commanders and men drill the sixty-four Sun Wu formations known as the maneuver.
Commanders and men drill the sixty-four formations of the Sun (Sunzi) and Wu (Wu Qi) arts of war known as the maneuver.
孫、吳 are two strategists, Sunzi and Wu Qi, not the single name Sun Wu.
The Grand Commandant, credential in hand, presents the regalia with the Director of the Imperial Clan as deputy, raising the Honored Lady to empress.
Grand Commandant Xi, credential in hand, presents the regalia with the Director of the Imperial Clan Zu as deputy, raising the Honored Lady to empress.
The edict names the envoys 太尉襲 and 宗正祖.
At autumn's advent they greet yellow qi in the southern suburb with Yellow Bell music, the hymn "Imperial Presence," shield dances, and the Cloud and Nurture dances to tune the season.
At autumn's advent they greet yellow qi at the yellow suburb with Yellow Bell music, the hymn "Imperial Presence," shield dances, and the Cloud and Nurture dances to tune the season.
黃郊 is the yellow (central) suburban altar, not the southern suburb.
The Chu Liu opens with Forester Yu; once officers announce readiness they rotate inward and loose at the beast.
The Chu Liu opens with a sacrifice to the First Forester (先虞); once officers announce readiness they rotate inward and loose at the beast.
先虞 is the ancestral spirit of hunting/foresters, not a person named Yu.
The emperor rides the martial avenue on a white horse with crimson mane and personally bolts the quarry with a crossbow.
The emperor rides the war chariot on a white horse with crimson mane and personally bolts the quarry with a crossbow.
戎路 is the war chariot.
Han followed Qin by drilling chiefly in the tenth month at Chang'an's south gate with the five camps wheeling through eight arrays.

Han followed Qin: no drills in three seasons, only in the tenth month the emperor went to the south gate of Chang'an by the river, assembled the troops of the five camps and ran the eight formations, called 'chengzhi'.
Omits 三時不講 (no drills in three seasons), 車駕幸 (the emperor's visit) and the name 乘之.
Ancient and Modern Notes says: "Eighth year of Jianwu Beginning of Spring, grant dukes fifteen bolts, ministers ten bolts."
Ancient and Modern Notes says: "At the Beginning of Spring in Jianwu 8, grant dukes fifteen bolts, ministers ten bolts."
Clarifies the date phrase (建武八年立春).
[One] Comment [one] Gao Tang Long says: 'Emperors each take their phase's flourishing as zu ancestor sacrifice, its ending as la.
[One] Comment [one] Gaotang Long says: 'Emperors each take their phase's flourishing as zu ancestor sacrifice, its ending as la.
高堂隆 has the compound surname Gaotang; the given name is Long.
The Fire phase holds zu at noon and la at dog hour."
Fire is born in yin, flourishes in wu and ends in xu, so the fire house holds zu on wu days and la on xu days."
午 and 戌 are cyclical day signs, not hours; the translation also drops the yin/wu/xu sequence.
Han follows noon zu and dog-hour la.
Han follows zu on wu days and la on xu days.
午/戌 denote cyclical days, not hours.
Su Qin's fable says: 'A clay doll spoke to a peach emblem: Now you are peach wood from the eastern lands, carved into a human figure.'
Su Qin, persuading Lord Mengchang, said: 'A clay doll spoke to a peach emblem: Now you are peach wood from the eastern lands, carved into a human figure.'
蘇秦說孟嘗君: the addressee Lord Mengchang is omitted.
Comment [eight] Han Official Ranks says: "Grand general, Three Excellencies—la grant cash thirty thousand each, beef two hundred jin, polished rice two hundred hu;
Comment [eight] Han Official Ranks says: "Grand general, Three Excellencies—la grant cash three hundred thousand each, beef two hundred jin, polished rice two hundred hu;
special marquises one hundred fifty thousand;
They cage the rain god and drown the drought goddess.
They imprison Gengfu in the clear cold pool and drown Nüba in the divine pond.
耕父 is a drought ghost (see s0501), not a rain god; place names omitted.
Comment [four] Cai Zhi Han Observances says: "First month dawn—Son of Heaven favors Deyang Hall—leans balustrade.
Comment [four] Cai Zhi Han Observances says: "First month dawn—the Son of Heaven goes to the Deyang Hall and comes to the balcony.
幸 here means the emperor's visit, not 'favours'.
Han New Year audiences revived bi discs and pelts.
Han and Wei roughly followed this system: at the New Year assembly the lords held jade bi presented on deer skins, and ministers and below held what the ancient rites prescribe.
Heavily condensed; omits Wei and the ministers' gifts.
Hu Guang explains monthly audiences shrank to sixth and tenth new moons.
Hu Guang said: 'Under the old rites ministers attended court every month; the late emperor, finding this too frequent, cut it to the first days of the sixth and tenth months.
Omits 先帝 (the late emperor) as the one who reduced the audiences.
Cai Yong Record of Rites and Music says: "Han music four grades: first called Grand Harmonizer music—presiding suburban temples ascending tomb hall various meal-raising music.
Cai Yong's Treatise on Rites and Music says: "Han music four grades: first called Grand Harmonizer music—presiding suburban temples ascending tomb hall various meal-raising music.
禮樂志 is Cai Yong's treatise, not the Record of Rites.

Page 3121, line 6: "in the sixth year of Yuanchu, in the third month." Note: Lu Yun observes that according to Emperor An's Annals, in the third year of Yongchu, in the fourth month, on bingyin, Xia Qin, Chamberlain for Dependencies, became Minister over the Masses.

Page 3121, line 6: "in the sixth year of Yuanchu, in the third month." Note: Lu says, that according to Emperor An's Annals, in the third year of Yongchu, in the fourth month, on bingyin, Xia Qin, Chamberlain for Dependencies, became Minister over the Masses.
盧雲 means 'Lu (Wenchao) says'; 雲 (for 云) is the verb, not part of a name 'Lu Yun'.
Liu’s point is that “first” is impossible once the Secretariat had become the Central Herald office; the graph should not read jia.

The Collation Supplement cites Liu Congchen: in Jianshi 4 Emperor Cheng abolished the Secretariat (eunuch) office, making the Secretariat the Palace Herald Director (per the Han Old Observances), so the reading jia is wrong.
Omits Liu Congchen's full name, Emperor Cheng, Jianshi 4 and the source cited.
Qian flags a mismatch between the marriage edict and Wenren Xi’s tenure.
Qian Daxin notes that per the Annals of Emperor Ling, Grand Commandant Wenren Xi was dismissed in the third month, whereas the empress was invested in the seventh; perhaps the Annals' month is wrong.
Heavily condensed; omits the dates and the Annals.
The chronology implies Liu Kai replaces Xia Qin only under a Yuanchu dating.
If it were the Yuanchu era, Liu Kai had already replaced Xia Qin.
若元初時，劉愷乃代勤者: in Yuanchu Liu Kai had already succeeded Qin, so the Yuanchu 6 date of the patent is doubtful.
Qian notes that the Annals of Emperor Ling read "seventh month, guichou day" for the same ceremony.
The Jijie cites Qian Daxin, who notes that the Annals of Emperor Ling read "seventh month, guichou day" for the same ceremony.
Qian Daxin's full name and the Jijie citation are omitted.
Folio 3129, line 1: ‘First name Mu[lacuna]’—Comment: Ji and Palace editions show a lacuna for another lacuna; Lu Wencha follows the Guoyu Wei commentary in reading zhong ‘swelling demon.’
Folio 3129, line 1: ‘First name Mu[lacuna]’—Comment: Ji and Palace editions show a lacuna for another lacuna; Lu Wenchao follows the Guoyu Wei commentary in reading zhong ‘swelling demon.’
盧文弨 is Lu Wenchao; the final syllable is truncated.
Folio 3129, line 12: ‘Each Minister of Education receives five thousand’—Comment: Lu suspects the word shi ‘clerk’ dropped after ‘minister.’
Folio 3129, line 12: ‘The Director of the Masters of Writing each receives five thousand’—Comment: Lu suspects the word shi ‘clerk’ dropped after ‘director’ (令).
尚書令 is the Director of the Masters of Writing, not the Minister of Education.
The surname was miscopied as chen ‘minister.’
Here Liu Zhao quotes Wei Zhao's commentary on the Guoyu; 臣 should be 韋.
Omits that Liu Zhao is quoting Wei Zhao's Guoyu commentary.
Witnesses disagree on whether the clause repeats ‘gate’ or uses ‘beyond.’
The Jijie cites Huang Shan: Qin Huitian, following an old edition, reads 之外 for 門外.
Omits the scholars named (Huang Shan, Qin Huitian).
(Lu's emendation, completed in the next note:) east
The source here has only the emended graphs 位 and 東; Lu is named in the continuation (s0872).

unresolvedReferences.description: The Chunqiu Fanlu quotation (s0020-s0036) is attributed to the book, not to Dong Zhongshu by name; no author claim is made from it.
應龍 (the Responsive Dragon) is a mythical creature and is not extracted as a person.
The Model Sayings (法言) is Yang Xiong's work, but he is not named; not extracted.
The answer (曰) to Huan Tan's question is presumably Liu Xin's, but the speaker is not named.
The emperor speaking as 朕 in Xia Qin's Yuanchu 6 patent (Emperor An) is not named.
成帝三年 is taken as Jianshi 3 (c. 30 BC); the reign-year count is ambiguous by one year, so an interval (31-30 BC) is given.
The rites for investing the crown prince and enfeoffing kings and dukes use placeholders (某) only; no person identified.
朕 in the edict (Emperor Ling) is a pronoun and not linked; the emperor is linked via 天子 in s0257.
The Monthly Ordinance Commentary (月令章句) and Solitary Judgments (獨斷) are Cai Yong's works; he is not named.
The Lüshi chunqiu is cited without naming Lü Buwei.
The Jianwu 8 (AD 32) grant of silk is dated by Emperor Guangwu's era, but no person is named.
乘輿 (the emperor) at the solstice music rite is generic; not linked.
The twelve exorcising spirits of the nuo chant (Jiazuo, Feiwei, Xiongbo, Tengjian, Lanzhu, Boqi, Qiangliang, Zuming, Weisui, Cuoduan, Qiongqi, Tenggen) are spirits, not people; not extracted.
乘輿 (the emperor) at the nuo rite is generic; not linked.
Zhuanxu's three sons (plague ghosts) are unnamed; no family edge created.
Demons and spirits (chimei, yukuang, weiyi, Fangliang, Gengfu, Nüba, kui, wangxiang, Youguang, □zhong) are not extracted as people.
Pi Cang (埤蒼) is cited by title; its author Zhang Yi is not named.
The Decisions on Doubtful Points (決疑要注) is cited by title; its author (Zhi Yu) is not named.
皇帝/天子 at the New Year audience are generic; not linked.
先帝 (the late emperor) who reduced the monthly audiences is not named.
The Xiping 4 (175) issue of the Yuntai poems was under Emperor Ling, who is not named.
汲本/毛本 (the Jiguge edition of Mao Jin) are cited as editions; Mao Jin is not extracted.

Xia Qin's appointment is dated Yuanchu 6 (119) in Ding Fu's patent (chunk 004) but Yongchu 3 (109) in the Annals of Emperor An cited here; both dates are recorded on their own evidence, and the conflict is left open.
Wenren Xi is identified here with the 太尉襲 of the Jianning 4 edict (chunk 005), but his dismissal in the third month conflicts with the seventh-month investiture.
The Han Feizi (韓非子) is cited as a book; Han Fei is not extracted as a person.
